title: NURS 1017 Unit 7 Case Study 9

question.stem: The nurse reviews the Nurses' Notes. Highlight the findings that may have contributed to the client's seizure.
question.explanation:
Possible contributors (triggers):

Missed antiseizure medication: the most common cause of a breakthrough seizure. Levetiracetam levels fall within a day or two of stopping it.

Sleep deprivation: one of the strongest seizure triggers; exam periods are a common time for breakthrough seizures in students.

Alcohol: heavy drinking, and the withdrawal period the next day, lower the seizure threshold.

Skipped meals: low blood glucose and missed routines can trigger seizures.

Not contributors here: a usual amount of coffee, ordinary lighting (flashing or flickering lights affect only people with photosensitive epilepsy) and regular exercise. The tongue bite is a result of the seizure, not a cause.

What a seizure is: a sudden, abnormal, excessive electrical discharge of a group of neurons that changes movement, sensation, awareness or behaviour. Epilepsy is a tendency to have recurrent unprovoked seizures.

leftContent.intro: The nurse on a medical unit is caring for a 20-year-old female university student with epilepsy.

question.stem: The client's roommate has witnessed several of her seizures and describes them to the nurse. For each description, click to specify the type of seizure it is most consistent with.

rows.text: “She gets a rising feeling in her stomach and smells burning rubber, but she can still talk to me.”
“She stiffens, falls, and her arms and legs jerk; afterwards she's confused and sleeps for an hour.”
“She stares, smacks her lips, and fiddles with her sleeve; she doesn't answer me and doesn't remember it later.”
“When she was a child, she would stare blankly for a few seconds many times a day, then carry on as if nothing happened.”
“Her right hand twitches for about a minute, and she watches it happen and tells me about it.”

question.explanation:
Accurate observation and description help the provider classify seizures and guide treatment and safety teaching. Seizures are focal (starting in one area of the brain) or generalized (involving both sides from the start).

Focal aware: the person stays aware. It may be a sensation (a rising feeling in the stomach, an unusual smell) or movement of one part of the body. A focal aware seizure that comes before a larger seizure is often called an aura, and it is documented.

Focal impaired awareness: the person is confused or unaware, often with staring and automatisms (lip smacking, fumbling), and does not remember it afterwards. A focal seizure can spread to both sides and become a tonic-clonic seizure.

Generalized tonic-clonic: stiffening (tonic phase) and a fall, then rhythmic jerking (clonic phase), often with tongue biting and incontinence, followed by a postictal period of confusion, headache, sore muscles and sleepiness.

Absence: brief (seconds) staring spells, often many times a day, with immediate recovery; most common in children.

Phases: prodrome (warning signs hours before, such as irritability), ictal (the seizure itself) and postictal (recovery).

cloze.text: While the client is in hospital, the nurse's priority problem is [[drop0]] because [[drop1]]. Before discharge, the nurse's teaching will focus first on [[drop2]].

options.text: her levetiracetam levels are low, so another seizure may occur
taking her antiseizure medication every day without running out

question.explanation:
Risk for injury and aspiration: until her medication level is restored, she may have another seizure. During a tonic-clonic seizure she could fall, strike her head or limbs, or aspirate saliva or vomit, so safety is the first priority.

Teaching priority: running out of medication was the main trigger; daily adherence, refills before the supply ends, and a plan for missed doses prevent most breakthrough seizures. Sleep, alcohol and meals are taught next. Caffeine in moderation, ordinary lighting and exercise are not problems for her.

question.stem: Which interventions should the nurse include when setting up seizure precautions for the client? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep oxygen and suction equipment ready at the bedside
Tape a padded tongue blade to the head of the bed
Take her temperature with an oral glass thermometer
Have her shower with the bathroom door unlocked and a nurse nearby, rather than take a tub bath
Remove nearby objects that could injure her, such as the bedside table
Apply wrist restraints while she sleeps
Keep the bed in the lowest position with the side rails up and padded

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Provider Orders.
question.explanation:
Include: a low bed with padded rails prevents falls and injury. Oxygen and suction support the airway after a seizure. A patent IV lets the nurse give lorazepam quickly if a seizure lasts 5 minutes or more. Showers with someone nearby are safer than tub baths (drowning risk). Hazards near the bed are moved away.

Do not include: nothing is placed in the mouth during a seizure; a tongue blade can break teeth, cause airway obstruction or injure the nurse. Oral temperatures are avoided, especially with glass or breakable thermometers, because she could bite down during a seizure; tympanic, temporal or axillary routes are used. Restraints cause injury and are not used.

question.stem: Complete the diagram by dragging from the choices below to specify what condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take to address that condition, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor to assess the client's progress.
question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 2 0610.
question.explanation:
Condition: the smell of burning rubber (an aura, a focal aware seizure) followed by loss of consciousness, stiffening and rhythmic jerking of all limbs is a focal seizure that spread to a bilateral tonic-clonic seizure.

Actions: turning her onto her side lets saliva drain and keeps the tongue from blocking the airway; a pillow or padding protects her head. Timing the seizure is essential: a seizure lasting 5 minutes or more is an emergency, and the prescribed lorazepam is given. Nothing is put in the mouth, and her movements are not restrained (injury risk). Nothing is given by mouth until she is fully awake and can swallow.

Parameters: airway and breathing (respiratory pattern, oxygen saturation; suction and oxygen as needed) and level of consciousness and orientation through the postictal period (asking her name and location). The nurse documents the aura, time of onset, the movements, duration, incontinence or injury, and the length of the postictal period, and notifies the provider.

question.stem: For each statement, click to specify whether it indicates an understanding of the teaching or a need for further teaching.

rows.text: Client: “I'll set alarms on my phone for my levetiracetam and refill it a week before I run out.”
Client: “If I miss a dose, I'll just take two at the next dose.”
Client: “I won't drive until my neurologist tells me it's safe under the provincial rules.”
Client: “I can stay up all night studying as long as I take my pills.”
Roommate: “If she has a seizure, I'll turn her on her side, time it, and call 9-1-1 if it lasts 5 minutes.”
Client: “I'll swim only with a friend who knows about my epilepsy.”
Client: “I'll wear my medical alert bracelet.”

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 2 0614 and Day 3 1000.
question.explanation:
Understanding: reminders and early refills support adherence, the most important way to prevent seizures. In Canada, provincial licensing rules restrict driving after a seizure; the neurologist advises when she may drive. Friends who know seizure first aid (side-lying, timing, call 9-1-1 at 5 minutes, or if she is injured or does not wake up) keep her safe. Swimming with a knowledgeable companion and wearing a medical alert bracelet are standard safety measures.

Needs further teaching: doubling a missed dose can cause side effects (drowsiness, dizziness); she follows the pharmacist's instructions, usually taking the missed dose when she remembers unless the next one is due soon. Sleep deprivation is a trigger even when medications are taken; regular sleep is part of seizure control. The nurse also offers support for coping with stigma and with exam stress (campus health services, Epilepsy Canada resources).
